title: A Bronze Ring Left High on an Alpine Pass
dek: At 2,600 metres on the Lötschen Pass, archaeologists found a 4,000-year-old bronze neck ring in near-perfect condition, wedged against a rock far from any known site.
body: The ring was lying against a rock, vegetation growing around it, roughly 13 centimetres across with two looped ends. It is bronze, and it is almost four thousand years old. Archaeologists from the Archaeological Service of the Canton of Bern found it in October 2026 at the Lötschen Pass, high in the Swiss Alps, in an area where no artefacts had ever been recorded.

The pass sits at about 2,600 metres above sea level and has carried people across the Alps for thousands of years. It links the Bernese Oberland with the Valais. The ring dates to between 2000 and 1700 BC, the Early Bronze Age. It is the first bronze object and the first piece of jewellery from that period found at the pass, and it survives in remarkably good condition despite its age and delicate construction.

The pass has a long record of travellers. Previous finds there include Roman coins, medieval arrows, Bronze Age arrows and bows, and a chip-carved wooden box. Each object marks someone who crossed. The new ring is older than most of them, and it belonged to a person, worn around the neck rather than carried as a tool or a weapon.

Similar neck ornaments are known from Early Bronze Age graves at Gwatt, Einigen and Hilterfingen, where examples have been found in both male and female burials. Contemporary sites are also known south of the Bernese Alps in the Valais. The find at Lötschen therefore adds another piece of evidence for movement between communities on opposite sides of the mountains in the Early Bronze Age.

What makes the ring interesting is where it was left. It sat some distance from the previously known archaeological concentrations at the pass, isolated, not dropped among the debris of a camp. That has led the archaeologists to consider whether it was deliberately deposited rather than simply lost during a journey. One possibility they raise is an offering to a deity, perhaps by someone asking for protection before crossing or giving thanks after arriving.

The find also shows the race archaeologists run in the high Alps. Artefacts preserved for centuries beneath ice can deteriorate rapidly once exposed, especially organic materials like wood and leather. The Archaeological Service regularly monitors Alpine sites so newly exposed objects can be documented and recovered before they are damaged or lost. This ring was recovered in time.

The neck ring has now been transferred to the Archaeological Service laboratories in Bern, where it will undergo further examination and conservation. Whatever the reason for its deposition, it shows that people were carrying valuable personal objects across high Alpine routes almost four millennia ago, long before the Roman and medieval travellers whose possessions have also been found there.
doesnt_show: It does not show who left the ring, why, or whether the deposit was ritual rather than accidental; the offering idea is one possibility the archaeologists are considering, not a conclusion.
settle: Laboratory examination of the ring and the surrounding soil for wear, residue or associated deposits could clarify whether it was worn, carried and deliberately placed.
